ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Above the horizontally fixed screen MN, there is a uniform magnetic field with magnetic induction strength B, directed perpendicularly into the plane of the paper. P is a particle source on the screen, continuously emitting particles with mass m and charge -q (q > 0) at the same velocity. These particles are injected into the magnetic field region from P in a direction perpendicular to the magnetic field. PC is perpendicular to MN, and the direction of particle incidence spreads within an angle of $\theta=60^{\circ}$ with respect to PC. EF is a charge collection plate parallel and opposite to MN, and EF can move freely up and down. Initially, EF is far enough from MN that no particles hit the plate. Now, EF is slowly moved downward, and when EF is at a distance d from MN, it just begins to collect charged particles. The gravitational force and interactions between the charged particles are neglected.

1. What is the velocity $v$ of the particle entering the magnetic field at point P?
2. After removing EF, what is the length L of the region on the screen MN where the particles hit?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the lower part of the figure there is a horizontal screen MN, and particle source P is located on MN; from P upward there is a vertical dashed line PC, and PC is perpendicular to MN. Above there is a horizontal collecting plate EF parallel to MN. The magnetic field region is represented by multiple “×” marks, indicating that the magnetic field is perpendicular to the page inward. Particles are injected from P, and the two upper boundary rays are distributed about PC; the angle between each boundary and PC is marked θ, the figure gives θ=60°, and the velocity direction is between these two boundaries. Reasoning: Take MN as the x-axis, P as the origin, and vertically upward as the y-axis. Let the angle between the initial velocity direction of the particle and PC be α, with rightward as positive, then α∈[-60°,60°]. The particle charge is -q, and the magnetic field is perpendicular to the page inward, so the particle undergoes uniform circular motion, with trajectory radius R=mv/(qB). According to the geometric relation of the method given in the problem, the coordinates of the circle center relative to P are (R cosα, -R sinα). Therefore the highest height that this circular trajectory can reach is the center height plus the radius: y_max= -R sinα+R=R(1-sinα). EF moves downward from far away; when it just starts collecting particles, the distance d from the plate to MN equals the maximum value among the highest points of all possible trajectories. Since y_max=R(1-sinα), in α∈[-60°,60°], it is maximum when α=-60°, so d=R(1+sin60°)=R(1+√3/2). Solving gives R=d/(1+√3/2)=2d/(2+√3)=2(2-√3)d. Also R=mv/(qB), so v=qBR/m=2(2-√3)qdB/m. After EF is removed, the particle trajectory intersects MN, namely y=0, again. The circle equation gives the horizontal coordinate of the second intersection point as x=2R cosα. When α changes from -60° to 60°, cosα changes from 1/2 to 1, therefore the range of x is [R,2R]. The length of the region hit on screen MN is L=2R-R=R=2(2-√3)d. Final answer: v=2(2-√3)qdB/m, L=2(2-√3)d.
